questions.prompt: Put these steps of signing in to your Oracle Fusion practice environment for the first time, per Lesson 1, in the correct order.
items: Open the sign-in URL OracleERPGuide provided
Enter the username and temporary password
Set a new password that meets Oracle's complexity rules
Land on the Oracle Fusion home page (the Springboard)
questions.explain: Lesson 1's sign-in checklist runs in this order: open the URL you were given, enter the username and temporary password, set a new password when Oracle forces the change, and only then do you land on the home page with its Navigator menu.

questions.prompt: A consultant needs to find the "Manage Chart of Accounts Structures" task but doesn't know which functional area it technically lives under. Per Lesson 2, what is the fastest way to find it in Setup and Maintenance?
options: Type "chart of accounts" into the search box at the top of Setup and Maintenance
Expand every functional area under the Financials offering one by one until it appears
Create a new implementation project scoped to the Financials offering first
Ask an administrator to move the task into a different functional area so it's easier to browse to
questions.explain: The search box surfaces every task whose name matches the typed phrase, regardless of which functional area it technically sits in. Lesson 2 calls this the fastest way to find a specific task once you know roughly what it's called, and the way most working consultants actually navigate day to day rather than drilling through the tree every time.

questions.prompt: Match each Setup and Maintenance term to what it actually is, per Lessons 2 and 4.
right: A logical grouping within an offering, such as Enterprise Profile or Ledger and Reporting Configuration
An individual, clickable configuration step, such as Manage Chart of Accounts Structures
A named, scoped bundle of generated setup tasks used to track a specific rollout
A large licensed product area, such as Financials or Procurement
questions.explain: An offering is a large licensed product area like Financials. Each offering breaks into functional areas, logical groupings like Enterprise Profile. Each functional area contains individual setup tasks, the actual clickable steps. An implementation project is the named, scoped container that bundles a generated task list for a specific rollout.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle's own guidance is to keep an implementation project scoped to no more than ________ offering wherever practical, since a project spanning multiple offerings is harder to export, import, and hand off between environments.
questions.explain: Lesson 4 is explicit that Oracle recommends scoping an implementation project to no more than one offering wherever practical, specifically because multi-offering projects are harder to export, import, and hand off between environments like test and production.

questions.prompt: During setup, a business unit gets assigned to the wrong legal entity by mistake. Per Lesson 3's overview of how enterprise structures connect, what actually happens to that business unit's transactions?
options: Every transaction that business unit processes posts to the wrong set of books
Nothing — business unit-to-legal-entity assignment is cosmetic and doesn't affect posting
The business unit is automatically prevented from processing any further transactions
Oracle Fusion silently reassigns the business unit to the correct legal entity the next time someone logs in
questions.explain: Lesson 3 is direct about this: "Get this wrong — for example, assign the wrong business unit to the wrong legal entity — and every transaction that business unit processes posts to the wrong set of books." Oracle Fusion doesn't detect or auto-correct this; it's exactly why enterprise structure design happens carefully, before any real transaction is entered.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a secondary ledger from a reporting currency, per Lesson 7?
options: A secondary ledger can represent an alternative accounting method, chart of accounts, or calendar from its primary ledger, while a reporting currency only restates the same ledger's data in another currency.

A reporting currency can represent an alternative accounting method, chart of accounts, or calendar from its primary ledger, while a secondary ledger only restates the same ledger's data in another currency.
A secondary ledger is mandatory for every accounting configuration, the same as a primary ledger, while a reporting currency is always optional.
A secondary ledger and a reporting currency are two different names for the exact same structure, chosen based on which subledger originated the transaction.
A reporting currency requires its own separate chart of accounts, while a secondary ledger must always share the primary ledger's chart of accounts.
Both a secondary ledger and a reporting currency must already exist before a primary ledger can be created.
questions.explain: A secondary ledger is optional and always tied to a primary ledger, but it can differ from that primary ledger in chart of accounts, calendar or period type, currency, or subledger accounting method — any one or more of the ledger's "4 Cs." A reporting currency is also optional, but it is strictly a currency restatement: the same primary or secondary ledger's data, shown in another currency, with no separate accounting method or chart of accounts of its own — "the same book, translated," not a different book.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the right shape of answer but swaps which structure does what: it's the secondary ledger that can carry a different accounting method, chart of accounts, or calendar, while the reporting currency is the one limited to restating the same ledger's data in another currency. Reversing those two roles is exactly the mix-up Lesson 7 warns against.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the moment you register a legal entity in Oracle Fusion, it automatically creates a matching ________, using the same name as the entity.
questions.explain: Lesson 6 covers this directly: registering a legal entity automatically creates a legal reporting unit (LRU) with the same name, the lowest-level component of a legal structure that requires its own registration for a given statutory or tax obligation.

questions.prompt: A consultant tries to register a brand-new legal entity, and the registration fails because something it depends on doesn't exist yet. Per Lesson 6, what is most likely missing?
options: A legal address for that entity, created first through Manage Legal Address
A primary ledger already assigned to that entity
A business unit already associated with that entity
A chart of accounts structure already deployed for that entity
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit that a legal entity's legal address must already exist, created through Manage Legal Address, before the entity can be registered — Oracle Fusion will not let you register a legal entity floating in space with no registered address, because no real legal entity exists without one.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Accounting Configuration Manager's guided flow, per Lesson 9, in the correct order.
items: Create or select the primary ledger and assign its chart of accounts, calendar, currency, and accounting method
Specify ledger options, such as journal sequencing, rounding, and approval rules
Assign the legal entities this ledger will account for
Assign or review balancing segment values per legal entity
Assign business units to the ledger
questions.explain: The Accounting Configuration Manager walks a consultant from creating the primary ledger (with its chart of accounts, calendar, currency, and accounting method already attached), through ledger options, to assigning legal entities, mapping each one's balancing segment values, and finally assigning business units — the same order Lesson 9 walks through.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ledger sets, per Lesson 8.
options: Every ledger in a ledger set must share the same chart of accounts and the same calendar or period type combination
A ledger set merges its member ledgers' balances into one new, combined accounting entity
A ledger set can simplify opening or closing an accounting period across every member ledger at once
A ledger set's members can include primary ledgers, secondary ledgers, and reporting currencies
Two ledgers using different charts of accounts can still be added to the same ledger set, as long as their calendars match
questions.explain: Ledger set membership has one hard requirement: identical chart of accounts and identical calendar/period type across every member, and members can be primary ledgers, secondary ledgers, or reporting currencies. Ledger sets simplify period opening/closing and reporting across their members, but each ledger keeps its own balances — a ledger set is a management and reporting convenience, not a new accounting entity that merges data. Differing charts of accounts disqualify a ledger from the set regardless of whether the calendars match.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about business functions and the shared service provider pattern, per Lesson 11.
options: A business unit can be assigned more than one business function, such as both Payables Invoicing and Requisitioning
A business unit with no Payables Invoicing function assigned will still show Payables-specific setup options, just left blank
In a shared service model, one business unit can act as the service provider for a specific function, while other business units become its client for that same function
Business function assignment is purely descriptive metadata with no effect on which setup tasks appear

Shared service centralizes a function like Payables Invoicing into one business unit that processes invoices on behalf of several operating business units, even though those operating units keep their own ledger and legal entity context for everything else
questions.explain: A business unit is not limited to one function — it can hold several. The shared service pattern designates one business unit as the service provider for a function, with others as its clients for that same function, exactly the centralized-AP-team example Lesson 11 describes, while the client units keep their own ledger and legal entity context for everything else. Function assignment is not cosmetic: a business unit with no Payables Invoicing function assigned shows no Payables-specific setup or reference data options at all, not blank ones.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle Fusion provides a special, predefined reference data set, often called the ________ Set (or Enterprise Set), for data that should be visible to every business unit regardless of which specific set they're otherwise assigned.
questions.explain: Lesson 12 names this the Common Set (or Enterprise Set) — the predefined set used for reference data that genuinely should be shared across every business unit, as opposed to data that needs to vary by business unit in its own named set.

questions.prompt: A consultant opens a reference data object's setup task and finds that it only offers the Common Set, with no determinant type and no option to create additional sets. Per Lesson 13, what does this tell the consultant?
options: That reference data object is not partitioned — every business unit sees the exact same values, and there's no "choice" to make
The object is partitioned by business unit, but the business units simply haven't been assigned to their own sets yet
The consultant needs to manually create a determinant type before the object can be used at all
The object is partitioned by ledger instead of business unit, which is why business unit doesn't appear as an option
questions.explain: Lesson 13's practical check is exactly this: if a reference data object's setup task only shows the Common Set with no determinant type and no way to create additional sets, it is non-partitioned, full stop — that object type simply was not designed to vary by business unit, ledger, or anything else.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually is, per Lessons 13 and 14.
right: The hierarchical structure (country, state, city, postal code) that validates and standardizes every address
A general-purpose, reusable address record used for offices, shipping points, or HR work sites
A value from a transaction's context, usually the business unit, that identifies which reference data set applies
The specific, formal address tied to a legal entity's registration
questions.explain: A legal address is the formal address tied to a legal entity's registration. A location is the general-purpose, reusable address record used anywhere Oracle Fusion needs "a place." A geography is the hierarchical structure that validates and standardizes every address entered. A determinant is the contextual value — usually business unit — that identifies which reference data set applies to a given transaction.

questions.prompt: Oracle Fusion's predefined geography data for a particular country is missing several state/province entries. Per Lesson 14, what is the most likely downstream consequence the first time someone enters an address in that country?
options: Validation errors, inconsistent formatting, or addresses that silently fail to map to the correct tax jurisdiction
The address entry screen becomes permanently locked for that entire country
Oracle Fusion automatically substitutes a default state for every address entered in that country
Nothing — geography data only affects reporting, never address entry itself
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is specific about this: incomplete or wrong geography data for a country means every address entered against that country inherits the problem — validation errors, inconsistent formatting, or addresses that silently fail to map to the correct tax jurisdiction. This is exactly why the lesson calls validating geography data a real step, not a formality.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a company defines twelve regular monthly periods, then adds one extra period at year-end used only to hold audit true-up entries. That extra period is called the ________ period.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 defines the adjusting period exactly this way: a special, additional period layered onto the regular calendar, used to isolate year-end audit adjustments or final closing entries from a normal operating period's day-to-day activity.

questions.prompt: A journal entry needs an exchange rate for a one-off situation where no automatic rate applies, so the preparer must type the rate in by hand during entry. Which conversion rate type is this, per Lesson 17?
options: User
Spot
Corporate
Fixed
questions.explain: User is the one exception to automation among the four predefined conversion rate types: when User is selected, Oracle Fusion does not supply a rate automatically, and the preparer must enter one manually. Spot, Corporate, and Fixed all supply a rate through normal, automated means.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about daily rates and cross rate rules, per Lesson 18.
options: A daily rate is specific to one currency pair, one conversion rate type, and one effective date
The Daily Rates Import and Calculation process can pull rates from an external feed and load them automatically
A cross rate rule derives a rate between two currencies by routing through a third currency when a direct rate isn't readily available
Cross rate rules are only useful for the USD/EUR currency pair, since those are the only currencies with quoted rates
Once daily rates are configured, they don't need further attention — they're a one-time setup step like a calendar
questions.explain: A daily rate is a specific numeric rate for one currency pair, one rate type, and one date. The Daily Rates Import and Calculation process can automate loading these from an external feed. A cross rate rule derives a rate between two currencies by routing through a known third currency (often USD) when no direct rate is available — most useful for less commonly traded pairs, not limited to USD/EUR. Unlike a calendar or chart of accounts structure, daily rates need fresh data every single day the business operates — they are explicitly not a one-time setup step.

questions.prompt: Put these five period statuses, per Lesson 19, in the order a period generally moves through over its lifetime.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 describes periods as generally moving left to right through these statuses: starting Never Opened (or Future Enterable, if posting ahead of schedule is needed), becoming Open when its time arrives, moving to Closed at month-end, and eventually Permanently Closed once no further changes will ever be needed.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants every accounting period to be the same length — commonly four or five weeks — instead of following irregular calendar months. Which calendar pattern, per Lesson 15, fits this requirement?
options: A 13-period calendar, often following a 4-4-5 week pattern across each quarter
A monthly Gregorian calendar
An adjusting-period-only calendar with no regular periods
A calendar with no period type defined
questions.explain: Lesson 15 describes 13-period calendars as the pattern used by companies, often retailers or manufacturers, that prefer equal-length accounting periods instead of irregular calendar months, frequently following a 4-4-5 week pattern across each quarter. A monthly Gregorian calendar instead follows twelve periods matching actual calendar months, which vary in length.

questions.prompt: A consultant wants to add the intercompany label to a segment that already carries the primary balancing label, to avoid creating an extra segment. Per Lesson 21, is this allowed?
options: No — a segment cannot carry the intercompany label and any balancing label at the same time, and the intercompany segment's value set must mirror the primary balancing segment's values
No — a segment cannot carry the intercompany label and the natural account label at the same time, though combining it with a balancing label is fine
Yes — any segment can carry the intercompany label alongside a balancing label, as long as the cost center label is left off that same segment
Yes — combining labels on one segment is always allowed in Oracle Fusion; label combinations are never restricted
No — the intercompany label can never be combined with the natural account label, which is the only restriction that applies to it
Yes — but only if the chart of accounts has fewer than four total segments
questions.explain: Lesson 21 states the intercompany label's one hard restriction directly: a segment carrying the intercompany label cannot also carry any of the three balancing labels (primary, second, or third), and its value set must mirror the primary balancing segment's values, since intercompany tracking is fundamentally about identifying which other entity a transaction is really with.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the right shape of answer — "no, there's a label conflict" — but names the wrong conflicting label. Lesson 21's restriction is specifically against combining the intercompany label with any balancing label; nothing in the lesson restricts combining intercompany with the natural account label.

questions.prompt: A value inside a Cost Center value set is marked Summary, with Posting Allowed turned off. What does this tell you about that value, per Lesson 22?
options: It's a parent/rollup value that reports can total up from its children, but transactions can't post to it directly
It's a disabled value that can no longer be used anywhere, including in reports
It's a dependent value whose availability depends on a value chosen in another segment
It's a table-validated value pulled live from another application table
questions.explain: Lesson 22 ties these two attributes together exactly this way: Summary marks a value as a parent/rollup value rather than one transactions post directly to, and a summary value typically has Posting Allowed turned off for that reason — transactions post to detail values, which then roll up into the summary for reporting.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a chart of accounts segment carrying the ________ label is mandatory and classifies every transaction into one of the five fundamental account types — asset, liability, equity, revenue, or expense.
questions.explain: Lesson 21 identifies the natural account label as mandatory, marking the segment that answers "what kind of thing is this, accounting-wise" — independent of which company, department, or product is involved.

questions.prompt: Match each value set validation type to what it actually does, per Lesson 22.
right: Values are pulled live from an existing application table
No fixed list; any value matching a format pattern is valid
A simple, standalone list that stands on its own
Valid values depend on a value already chosen elsewhere
questions.explain: Independent value sets are simple, standalone lists. Dependent value sets restrict valid choices based on a value already chosen in a related segment. Table-validated value sets pull their list live from an existing application table. Format Only value sets skip a fixed list entirely, validating only that an entered value matches a format pattern.

questions.prompt: A consultant wants a cross-validation rule's validation filter to automatically cover any new cost center added under the Manufacturing parent later, with no rule edit required. Per Lesson 24, what should the filter reference?
options: A hierarchy node (tree) for Manufacturing, instead of an exhaustive list of individual cost center values
A cross-validation combination set listing every current Manufacturing cost center by value
A format-only value set restricted to numeric cost centers
The Common reference data set assigned to the Manufacturing business unit
questions.explain: Lesson 24 is explicit that a cross-validation rule's condition or validation filter can reference a hierarchy node (tree) rather than an exhaustive list of individual values — a rule written against "all cost centers under the Manufacturing parent" automatically covers a new cost center added under that parent later, with no rule change required. A combination set, by contrast, is based on an explicit list and would need to be edited to add the new value.

questions.prompt: In LTV Manufacturing Corporation's worked chart of accounts design (Lesson 25), the fifth segment, Future, carries no label and has no values populated yet. Why include it at all?
options: So a genuinely new reporting need later only requires populating that segment's value set, not redesigning the whole structure
Because every Oracle Fusion chart of accounts is technically required to have exactly five segments
Because the natural account segment needs a backup segment in case its value set runs out of values
Because Future is where Oracle Fusion automatically stores disabled values
questions.explain: Lesson 25 explains the Future segment as a deliberate reservation: if a genuinely new reporting need appears later, such as a product line segment, the chart of accounts structure itself doesn't need to be redesigned from scratch — only the Future segment's value set needs to be populated. This is the same "simplest structure that satisfies today's requirements" principle from Lesson 5, applied with room for predictable growth.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of freezing and deploying a chart of accounts structure, per Lesson 26, in the correct order.
items: Define segments on the structure — count, order, labels, and widths
Create one or more structure instances, assigning actual value sets
Freeze and deploy each structure instance
questions.explain: Lesson 26 walks through this exact sequence: define the segments, freeze the structure definition to lock it against casual changes, deploy the structure to generate the database objects and make it available for use, create structure instances by assigning real value sets, and then freeze and deploy each instance so it becomes usable by a ledger. Both the structure and each instance go through their own freeze-and-deploy cycle.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about rapid implementation (RI) spreadsheets, per Lesson 27.
options: Rapid implementation spreadsheets can generate a chart of accounts, calendar, legal entities, and a primary ledger from filled-in templates
ADFdi and FBDI are tools used behind the scenes to connect the spreadsheets to Oracle Fusion and import the data
Rapid implementation is the recommended approach for a complex multinational with many legal entities and multiple charts of accounts
Even after a successful RI spreadsheet upload, a consultant should still manually verify segment labels and the balancing-segment-value-to-legal-entity mapping
Once an RI spreadsheet upload succeeds, no further review is needed before go-live
questions.explain: RI spreadsheets generate the chart of accounts, calendar, legal entities, primary ledger, and business units from filled-in templates, using ADFdi and FBDI-backed tools behind the scenes. Lesson 27 explicitly says RI is built for simple, single-chart-of-accounts, limited-entity requirements, not a complex multinational with many legal entities and multiple charts of accounts — and that even a successful upload is a starting point, requiring manual verification of segment labels, balancing-segment-value mapping, and cross-validation rules before go-live, not a substitute for that review.

questions.prompt: A consultant tests a new cross-validation rule by entering a known-good account combination and confirming it's accepted. Satisfied, they mark the rule as tested. Per Lesson 28, is this testing complete?
options: No — the rule also needs to be tested with a known-bad combination to confirm it's actually rejected
Yes — confirming a good combination is accepted is the only test a cross-validation rule needs
No — cross-validation rules can't be tested manually at all; only an audit can verify them
Yes — but only if the good combination was selected at random rather than chosen deliberately
questions.explain: Lesson 28 calls out exactly this shortcut: testing only the "it lets good combinations through" side and skipping the "it actually blocks bad ones" side is a common, costly mistake. A rule that has never actually rejected anything hasn't been tested, it's just been assumed to work — a rule configured backward or scoped to the wrong range will not announce the mistake itself.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 29, the single most damaging common mistake is failing to assign a primary ________ value to each legal entity, which silently breaks the ability to produce a clean trial balance per entity.
questions.explain: Lesson 29 names this as the single most damaging mistake on its list: skipping the balancing-segment-value-to-legal-entity assignment from Lesson 9 silently breaks the ability to produce a clean trial balance per legal entity, and it often isn't discovered until someone actually needs that separated report — usually at period close, under pressure, far later than when the mistake was made.
